opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think about it a lot. My intuition is that when you scale up to internet-scale data, you don't just get more of everything in proportion. You get an enormous amount of the common, the typical, the frequently photographed or frequently written about. The head of the distribution gets heavier, and the behavior that dominates the data is whatever people tend to capture and share most often.

Think about video, which is where a lot of my work has been. If you scrape video from the internet, you get a lot of people cooking, people talking to the camera, sports highlights, pets doing funny things. What you don't get nearly as much of are the subtle, mundane, long-duration activities that actually matter for a lot of real-world applications, like someone slowly assembling furniture, a technician doing a maintenance procedure, or the rare events in driving that matter most for safety. Those live in the long tail, and adding more internet data doesn't necessarily fill that tail. Sometimes it pushes it further out relative to the head.

So there's a seductive idea that scale washes out bias, that with enough data everything gets covered. I don't think that's right. Scale amplifies whatever the collection process favors. There's a selection effect in what people choose to record and post, and then a second one in how we filter and curate, often with models trained on earlier data, which reinforces the same patterns.

The practical upshot is that models trained this way get very good at the typical case and look impressive on benchmarks drawn from the same distribution, but they can be surprisingly brittle on the specific, less-represented behaviors you care about when you deploy them. That's why I keep coming back to the data itself: understanding what's in your dataset, where the gaps are, what's overrepresented, and being deliberate about curation instead of assuming more is better. Internet scale is incredibly powerful, but it's not a substitute for knowing what your data actually contains.

r001.rationale: The response says internet-scale data contains an even greater amount of common, typical behavior, making the distribution’s head heavier and those frequent behaviors dominant.

fable-5.1.text:
My intuition is that as you scale toward internet-scale data, the behavior that dominates isn't the interesting behavior, it's the common behavior. The long tail gets washed out. If you think about video in particular, which is where a lot of my work has been, the vast majority of what's uploaded is people doing fairly mundane things: talking to a camera, walking, cooking, playing with a pet. So the statistics of the data set end up being dominated by those modes, and a model trained on it becomes very good at the average case and surprisingly brittle on the things you might actually care about, the rare events, the unusual interactions, the edge cases.

There's also a subtler effect, which is that you're not sampling the world, you're sampling what people chose to record and chose to upload. That's a filtered view. It's biased toward what's visually interesting to humans, what's socially shareable, what certain demographics with certain devices tend to capture. So "internet-scale" sounds like it approximates reality, but it's really approximating a particular slice of human attention.

What I think that means practically is that scale alone doesn't solve the problem. You still need to be deliberate about curation, about understanding what's in your data and what's missing from it. In our work, a lot of the value came not from having more data but from having better-characterized data, where we actually knew the distribution of activities, viewpoints, and conditions. And I'd argue that as the data gets bigger, that understanding becomes more important, not less, because the dominant modes get more dominant and it gets harder to even notice what the model has never seen.

r001.rationale: The response says that as data scales up, common behavior dominates its statistics and models become good at the average case.

astra-6.text:
My intuition is that as we move toward internet-scale data sets, the common patterns become increasingly dominant. You get more examples of the things people tend to capture and share, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you get a more balanced picture of the world. There’s a selection process in what ends up on the internet.

So the question is whether we’re getting meaningful diversity or just more observations of the same dominant behaviors. The rare cases may increase in absolute number, but they can still contribute very little to the learning objective. Scale helps, but I wouldn’t assume that scale alone solves that problem.

r001.rationale: It says common patterns become increasingly dominant as datasets reach internet scale, directly expressing the target intuition.

sol-6.1.text: My intuition is that scale alone doesn’t necessarily give you diversity. As you move toward internet-scale data, you get more examples of the things people tend to record and share. Those common behaviors can dominate the data, while the unusual behaviors—the ones you might really care about detecting—remain relatively rare. So you may get very good at modeling the dominant patterns without getting much better at understanding the long tail. The question is not just how much data you have, but what that data actually represents.

r001.rationale: The response says that at internet scale, commonly recorded and shared behaviors can dominate the data, expressing the target intuition.
